summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the neglect adjudication, holding the State must prove neglect by a preponderance of the evidence, and cautioned that an officer taking warrantless protective custody under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-3-405(a)(i) must actually find the child seriously endangered rather than apply a blanket positive-drug-test policy.
key_cases.relevance: Describes the combined shelter-care and initial hearing that follows the filing of a neglect petition under § 14-3-409(c).
key_cases.quote: During the adjudicatory hearing, the State had the burden to prove its allegations of neglect by a preponderance of the evidence

key_cases.holding: The Court held that the statutory right to a jury trial at a juvenile adjudicatory hearing is waived unless a written demand is filed within ten days of the advisement, and affirmed the neglect adjudication as supported by sufficient evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Fixes the procedural consequences of the initial hearing on a neglect petition, including the ten-day jury demand.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that Mother waived her right to a jury trial when she failed to file a demand within the ten-day time frame required by statute

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding the juvenile court violated the father's due-process right to notice and an opportunity to be heard in the early stages of the case, and that 'other aggravating circumstances' relieving the Department of reasonable efforts under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 14-2-309(c)(v) must be as severe as the enumerated grounds.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the notice and hearing obligations that attach once the petition is filed and the case is opened.
key_cases.quote: the legislature logically meant for “other aggravating circumstances” to meet the same level of severity as set out in the preceding provisions

key_cases.case_name: JET v. State, Department of Family Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the refusal to let a young mother withdraw her admission of neglect, holding the juvenile court gave the statutorily required advisements at the initial hearing and did not abuse its discretion despite her claim of mental illness and her own earlier requests for help.
key_cases.relevance: Governs admissions entered on a neglect petition and the standard for withdrawing them.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court did not abuse its discretion in denying the appellant's motion to withdraw her admission of neglect

key_cases.holding: Over a two-justice dissent, the Court affirmed a juvenile-court adjudication of neglect and the ensuing placement order, holding that neglect need be shown only by a preponderance of the evidence and that the record contained sufficient evidence to sustain the finding under the statutory definition of a neglected child.
key_cases.relevance: The Court held the notice and opportunity to be heard due a parent after a neglect petition is filed are proportionate to the magnitude of the infringement, which is less than at a termination proceeding.
key_cases.quote: Child neglect, on the other hand, need only be shown by a preponderance of the evidence.

state_agency.name: Wyoming Department of Family Services
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the DFS field office in the county where the child lives — the list is at dfs.wyo.gov/about/contact-us

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately after the decree, or at a postponed hearing within 60 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Court or jury finds the child neglected after an adjudicatory hearing, a valid admission or a confession
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-426; subsection (e) lets the court continue a disposition hearing for a reasonable time not to exceed sixty (60) days
